hints: Recall that frequency counts how often a repeating event happens at one location in a progressive wave.
teacher_walkthrough: Frequency $f$ is defined as the number of complete oscillations per unit time.
For a progressive wave this is the number of wave cycles passing a fixed point per second, measured in hertz where $$1\,\text{Hz} = 1\,\text{s}^{-1}.$$
walkthrough: B1: number of oscillations / waves / crests passing a fixed point per unit time.
common_pitfalls: Confusing frequency with period or with wave speed; frequency is a rate, not a time or a distance.
Omitting per unit time; stating number of waves alone is insufficient for the mark.

hints: Measure the horizontal length of one complete cycle on Fig. 4.2 in cm and multiply by the time-base setting.
Use $f = 1/T$ and convert ms to s with $1\,\text{ms} = 10^{-3}\,\text{s}$ before evaluating.
teacher_walkthrough: Period $T$ is the time for one complete oscillation, obtained from horizontal distance on the CRO using $$T = \text{cycles length} \times \text{time-base}.$$
From Fig. 4.2 one full sine wave occupies $$4.0\,\text{cm}.$$
With time-base $0.50\,\text{ms}\,\text{cm}^{-1}$: $$T = 4.0 \times 0.50\,\text{ms} = 2.0\,\text{ms}.$$
Convert to seconds: $$T = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{s} = 0.0020\,\text{s}.$$
Frequency is $$f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{2.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 0.50 \times 10^{3} = 500\,\text{Hz}.$$
common_pitfalls: Miscounting the period as 2.0 cm or 8.0 cm instead of one full peak to peak distance of 4.0 cm.
Forgetting to convert ms to s, giving $f = 0.5$ or mishandling powers of 10.

formulas_used: V = \text{vertical height from centre line} \times y\text{-gain}
hints: Read the peak height from the central dashed line to a crest in cm, then multiply by the y-gain.
teacher_walkthrough: Voltage amplitude is peak displacement from equilibrium using $$V_0 = \text{amplitude in cm} \times y\text{-gain}.$$
From Fig. 4.2 peak height above centre line is $$2.8\,\text{cm}.$$
common_pitfalls: Using peak to trough height instead of peak to centre line, doubling the answer.
Confusing time-base with y-gain and multiplying cm by ms cm-1.

hints: Frequency is unchanged, so the sketched trace must keep the same period and same number of cycles in the same horizontal span.
Recall intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, so find the amplitude factor when intensity becomes $1/4$.
Combine the unchanged period with the new constant smaller amplitude centred on the same dashed line.
teacher_walkthrough: Intensity of a wave is proportional to the square of amplitude: $$I \propto A^{2}.$$
Given $$\frac{I_{new}}{I_{old}} = \frac{1}{4}$$ then $$\frac{A_{new}}{A_{old}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{4}} = \frac{1}{2}.$$
So CRO signal amplitude halves: $$A_{new} = \frac{2.8\,\text{cm}}{2} = 1.4\,\text{cm}.$$
Frequency is unchanged, so period and phase are unchanged.
Sketch: same sine shape with same 4.0 cm period aligned with original, but peaks at $1.4\,\text{cm}$ above and below the central dashed line throughout.
walkthrough: B1: same frequency / period / number of waves
common_pitfalls: Reducing amplitude to a quarter instead of a half by assuming $I \propto A$ linearly.
Changing the wavelength or shifting phase; only vertical scale changes.
Drawing decaying amplitude; the new intensity is constant, so amplitude is constant.

hints: State the condition of two or more waves overlapping at a point.
State the vector addition rule for resultant displacement at that point.
teacher_walkthrough: The principle of superposition governs overlap of waves.
When two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement at that point is the vector sum of the individual displacements of each wave.
walkthrough: B1: when two or more waves meet at a point
B1: resultant displacement is the sum of individual displacements
common_pitfalls: Referring to amplitude or intensity adding instead of displacement; superposition adds displacements.
Omitting that waves must meet or overlap; a single wave statement gains no credit.

hints: Identify amplitude minimum as a node and amplitude maximum as an antinode; count how many node to node intervals fit in 1.05 m.
Use node separation $\lambda/2$ to relate the total distance to wavelength.
teacher_walkthrough: In a stationary wave, amplitude minimum is a node and amplitude maximum is an antinode.
Successive nodes are separated by $$\frac{\lambda}{2}.$$
Motion from node to node passing through one maximum is one $\lambda/2$ interval.
Start node to end node passing through three maxima gives $$n = 3$$ intervals, so $$1.05\,\text{m} = 3 \times \frac{\lambda}{2}.$$
Hence $$\lambda = \frac{1.05 \times 2}{3} = \frac{2.10}{3} = 0.70\,\text{m}.$$
common_pitfalls: Using node to antinode $\lambda/4$ incorrectly or counting 3 wavelengths in 1.05 m.
Miscounting intervals as 3.5 or 6; sketch node, antinode, node sequence to verify 3 node to node gaps.

hints: Select the wave equation linking speed, frequency from (b)(i) and wavelength from (d)(ii).
Substitute values with consistent SI units of Hz and m to get m s-1.
teacher_walkthrough: Wave speed for a progressive wave is given by $$v = f\lambda.$$
Insert $f = 500\,\text{Hz}$ and $\lambda = 0.70\,\text{m}$: $$v = 500 \times 0.70.$$
Evaluate: $$500 \times 0.70 = 350.$$
common_pitfalls: Using period instead of frequency, computing $v = \lambda/T$ incorrectly with ms left unconverted.
Mixing up wavelength from a different part or using CRO cm values directly.
